{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=meta-reasoning+mechanisms+epistemic+boundaries+large+language+models+unrecognized+failure+modes&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"title\": [\"Structural Simulation Benchmark for Reasoning Large Language Models: Accuracy, Reliability, and Failure Modes\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large language models (LLMs), particularly reasoning-oriented models optimized for long-horizon and multi-step inference, are increasingly used to assist programming and scientific research. However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.62891/45c2ef5a\", \"title\": [\"Arkhe(N): Design Fiction as a Structured Method for Probing Epistemic Boundaries in Large Language Models\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.62891/45c2ef5a\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 2, 17]]…

{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.16021v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for
Effective Reasoning Support
DINITHI DISSANAYAKE, Augmented Human Lab, National University of Singapore, Singapore
SURANGA NANAYAKKARA, Augmented Human Lab, National University of Singapore, Singapore
Flow Theory describes an optimal cognitive state where individuals experience deep focus and intrinsic motivation when a task’s
difficulty aligns with their skill level. In AI-augmented reasoning, interventions that disrupt the state of cognitive flow can hinder rather
than enhance decision-making. This paper proposes a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework that adapts interventions
based on three key contextual factors: type, timing, and scale. By leveraging multimodal behavioral cues (e.g., gaze behavior, typing
hesitation, interaction speed), AI can dynamically adjust cognitive support to maintain or restore flow. We introduce the concept of
cognitive flow, an extension of flow theory in AI-augmented reasoning, where interventions are personalized, adaptive, and minimally
intrusive. By shifting from static interventions to context-aware augmentation, our approach ensures that AI systems support deep
engagement in complex decision-making and reasoning without disrupting cognitive immersion.
1 Introduction
The theory of flow, proposed by Csikszentmihalyi [ 3], defines an optimal psychological state in which individuals
experience deep focus and intrinsic motivation when the challenge of a task is perfectly matched to their skill level.
When a task is too easy, users become bored, while excessive difficulty leads to frustration. For example, in video games,
the enjoyment of a game depends on several factors, including the player’s skill level and the challenge the game
presents. A game that appropriately matches a player’s skill level fosters a sense of engagement, encouraging continued
play. Similarly, any new intervention or augmentation should support the user in either attaining or maintaining the
state of flow of whatever the current task the user is engaged in.
